We need to read the problem carefully. It is a modified problem compared to original: original asked number of servers that did NOT receive any requests in interval; modified asks number of servers that DID receive requests in interval.

Thus arr[i] = number of distinct server IDs that have at least one request in [queries[i] - x, queries[i]].

Given n servers (ids from 1 to n). We need to answer multiple queries each with interval of fixed length x+1 (inclusive endpoints). So each query's interval is [q - x, q].

We have up to 10^5 logs, queries length up to 10^5, n up to 10^5.

Goal: for each query count number of distinct server ids that appear in logs whose time falls in interval.

We can pre-process logs sorted by time, then sliding window approach: For each query sorted by q (i.e., by endpoint), we maintain a sliding window of logs whose time is within [q - x, q]. We need to maintain count of distinct server ids in current window. We'll add logs as we increase q (increase right endpoint) and remove logs as we move left bound forward (i.e., drop logs with time < q - x). For each query we answer distinct count.

That's straightforward: O((logs + queries) log (logs+queries)) for sorting and O(logs+queries) for sliding. Distinct count can be maintained with a frequency map: dict[server_id] -> count in window; and a variable distinct_count that increments when count goes from 0->1 and decrements when from 1->0.

Complexities: O((L+Q) log (L+Q) ) for sorting; O(L+Q) time for sliding; O(n) memory for freq (or O(L) but we can store up to n entries). Works.

Edge Cases: multiple logs for same server and time (like duplicate entries). Our freq will handle.

3. Sort queries_with_idx by q ascending.
